t.2.68.1: Having thus reproached his mother, Bharata, then seized by great anger, spoke these words once again.
t.2.68.4: By destroying this family you have incurred the sin of killing an unborn child. Kaikeyī, go to hell, and may you never share the same world as your husband!
t.2.68.3: What wrong did the king, or the exceedingly righteous Rāma, ever do to you, that death and exile have come upon the two of them alike because of you?
t.2.68.2: Be cast down from the kingdom, Kaikeyī, cruel woman of wicked conduct! Forsaken by dharma, do not stand weeping over the dead.
t.2.68.6: Because of you my father has passed away and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest, and by you I have been brought to infamy in the world of the living.
t.2.68.5: Since such a sin has been committed by you through this dreadful deed, casting off the one dear to all the world, fear has been brought even upon me.
t.2.68.8: Kausalyā and Sumitrā, and the other women who are my mothers, are overwhelmed by great sorrow, having encountered you, the defiler of our family.
t.2.68.7: O you who are my enemy in the guise of a mother, cruel woman lusting after the kingdom, I am not one to be spoken to by you, O wicked woman, slayer of your husband!
t.2.68.9: You are not the daughter of Aśvapati, that wise and righteous king; you are a rākṣasī born there, a destroyer of your father's family.
t.2.68.10: For by you the righteous Rāma, ever devoted to truth, was sent away to the forest, and father, out of grief, has gone to heaven.
t.2.68.11: That sin, of which you are the chief author, now rests upon me, bereft of my father, forsaken by my two brothers, and hateful to all the world.
t.2.68.12: Having, in your sinful resolve, left the righteous Kausalyā bereft, to what world will you go now, you who are headed for hell?
t.2.68.13: Cruel woman, why do you not recognize Rāma, the self-controlled refuge of his kinsmen, the eldest, equal to a father, the very son born of Kausalyā?
t.2.68.15: Once, it is said, Surabhi, knower of dharma and honored by the gods, saw on the earth her two sons, bearing the yoke, bereft of their senses.
t.2.68.14: A son is born from every limb and member, and from the heart as well; therefore he is dearer than the mother, but a kinsman is not, being dear only through affection.
t.2.68.16: Seeing those two sons lying exhausted on the ground at midday, I wept with grief for my son, my eyes brimming with tears.
t.2.68.17: As the great-souled king of the gods was passing beneath her, tiny drops of sweet fragrance from her fell upon his body.
t.2.68.18: Seeing that illustrious one consumed by grief, Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, king of the gods, distressed and with joined palms, spoke these words.
t.2.68.19: Surely there is no great danger of any kind threatening us from any quarter? Tell me, you who wish the welfare of all, what is the cause of your grief?
t.2.68.20: Thus addressed by the wise king of the gods, Surabhi, steadfast and skilled in speech, then replied with these words.
t.2.68.21: May evil be averted! No danger threatens you from any quarter, O lord of the immortals. But I grieve for my own two sons, sunk in misery and placed in a hard plight.
t.2.68.22: O lord of the gods, having seen these two wretched oxen at the plough, scorched by the rays of the sun and tormented by the ploughman…
t.2.68.23: Seeing these two, born from my own body, distressed and crushed beneath their burden, I am tormented with grief, for there is nothing as dear as a son.
t.2.68.24: Even the wish-fulfilling cow, who has thousands of sons, grieves; how much more, then, will Kausalyā, who must live on without Rāma?
t.2.68.25: This virtuous woman, who had but one son, has been made by you like a cow bereft of her calf; therefore you will reap unending sorrow, both here and after death.
t.2.68.26: For I shall surely pay this full homage to my brother and my father, and shall also increase their glory; of this there is no doubt.
t.2.68.27: Having had the son of Kausalyā, of great splendor, brought back, I myself will enter the forest frequented by sages.
t.2.68.29: Then the king's son, the scorcher of foes, his eyes reddened, his garments loosened, all his ornaments cast off, lay fallen upon the ground like the banner of Śacīpati at the close of the festival.
t.2.68.28: Speaking thus, like an elephant in the forest goaded by lance and hook, he fell to the ground, enraged, hissing like a serpent.
